questions.q: A class in C++ is best described as:

A blueprint or template that defines the properties and behaviors of objects
A built-in data type like int or float
A function that returns a value

The same as a class definition
A keyword used to declare variables

questions.q: A class definition in C++ typically ends with:
options: A closing brace followed by a semicolon
A closing brace with no semicolon

questions.q: Encapsulation in OOP refers to:
options: Bundling data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit, while restricting direct access to some components
Creating multiple objects from one class
Hiding a class from the linker
Allowing global access to all class members

questions.q: Encapsulation is primarily implemented in C++ using:
options: Access specifiers (private, protected, public) to control visibility of members

questions.q: Which of the following best demonstrates encapsulation?
options: Making all data members public for easy access
Making data members private and providing public getter/setter functions to access them
Declaring all functions as friend functions
Using global variables instead of class members

questions.q: The main benefit of encapsulation is:
options: Protecting an object's internal state from unintended or invalid external modification

Abstraction in OOP refers to:
options: Showing only essential features/behavior to the user while hiding implementation details
Combining data and functions into a class
Creating multiple copies of an object
Converting one data type to another

questions.q: A real-world analogy for abstraction is:
options: Driving a car using the steering wheel and pedals without needing to know the internal engine mechanics
Copying a class definition into another file
Using a for loop to iterate an array

questions.q: In C++, abstraction is commonly achieved using:
options: Abstract classes with pure virtual functions to define an interface

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes abstraction from encapsulation?
options: Abstraction focuses on hiding complexity/implementation details, while encapsulation focuses on bundling data with restricted access
They are exactly the same concept with different names
Abstraction is about memory allocation, encapsulation is about loops
Encapsulation hides implementation, abstraction restricts data access

questions.q: Abstraction helps developers primarily by:
options: Exposing all internal details of a class to the user
Reducing complexity by letting users interact with a simplified interface
Increasing the number of global variables

options: Multiple copies of the base class subobject are created

options: Function overriding through base class pointers

questions.q: Compile-time polymorphism is resolved:
options: By the compiler at compile time, based on function signatures

questions.q: Operator overloading, as a form of compile-time polymorphism, allows:
options: Operators to work only with built-in data types
Operators to be redefined to work with user-defined types like classes
The compiler to ignore operator precedence
Operators to be removed from the language

questions.q: Compared to compile-time polymorphism, run-time polymorphism generally:
options: Is faster because it avoids any lookup
Involves a small performance overhead due to dynamic dispatch via a vtable
Is not supported in C++ at all
Is resolved at compile time as well

questions.q: Function overloading achieves compile-time polymorphism by allowing:
options: The same function name to behave differently based on parameters, chosen by the compiler
Functions to be resolved only at runtime
Only one version of a function to exist
Functions to override base class behavior dynamically

questions.q: Run-time polymorphism in C++ is primarily achieved through:

options: A derived class provides a new implementation for a virtual function already defined in its base class, with the same signature
A function is defined twice with different parameters in the same class
A base class calls a derived class constructor
Two unrelated classes have functions with the same name

options: Always call the derived class version
Call the base class version regardless of the actual object type (no polymorphic behavior)

questions.q: Run-time polymorphism typically incurs a small overhead because:
options: The function call is resolved through a virtual table (vtable) lookup at runtime
The program must recompile at runtime

options: No, an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly; only derived concrete classes can be
Only if it has a constructor
Only if it has no data members

questions.q: A derived class that does not override all pure virtual functions inherited from an abstract base class:
options: Is not allowed to compile under any circumstances

questions.q: Pure virtual functions are primarily used to:
options: Provide a complete implementation that cannot be changed
Define an interface that derived classes must implement

questions.q: Which of the following is true about abstract classes in C++?
options: They can have both pure virtual functions and regular member functions with implementations
They cannot have any data members
They cannot be used as base classes

questions.q: A default constructor in C++ is a constructor that:
options: Takes at least one mandatory parameter
Takes no parameters (or has all parameters defaulted)
Can only be used for abstract classes

questions.q: A parameterized constructor allows:
options: Initializing object data members with values passed as arguments during object creation
Only default initialization of data members

questions.q: A copy constructor is used to:
options: Initialize a new object as a copy of an existing object of the same class
Convert a class into a template

questions.q: Which statement about destructors is correct?
options: A destructor can take parameters and be overloaded
A destructor takes no parameters, cannot be overloaded, and has the same name as the class prefixed with a tilde (~)
A destructor must always be declared static
A class can have multiple destructors with different signatures

questions.q: Unlike constructors, destructors:
options: Can be declared virtual, which is important for proper cleanup in inheritance hierarchies
Can never be virtual under any circumstances
Must always take one integer parameter
Are called before the object's constructor

questions.q: If a class does not explicitly define a constructor, the compiler:
options: Leaves the object completely uninitialized with no constructor at all

questions.q: The order in which a destructor is called relative to the object's scope is:
options: Destructors are called in the same order as constructors
Destructors are typically called in the reverse order of construction, when the object goes out of scope or is deleted

sections.name: Constructor Overloading & Order of Ctor/Dtor Calls in Inheritance

questions.q: Constructor overloading refers to:
options: Having multiple constructors in a class with different parameter lists
Having only one constructor per class

questions.q: When an object of a derived class is created, the order of constructor calls is typically:
options: The derived class constructor runs first, then the base class constructor
The base class constructor runs first, followed by the derived class constructor
Only the derived class constructor runs

questions.q: When an object of a derived class is destroyed, the order of destructor calls is typically:
options: The derived class destructor runs first, followed by the base class destructor (reverse of construction order)
The base class destructor runs first, followed by the derived class destructor
Only the base class destructor runs

questions.q: If a derived class does not explicitly call a specific base class constructor, which base class constructor is invoked by default?
options: The parameterized constructor with the most arguments

questions.q: To explicitly call a specific parameterized base class constructor from a derived class, you typically use:
options: An initializer list in the derived class constructor

questions.q: Constructor overloading is a specific application of which broader OOP concept?
Operator overloading in C++ allows:
options: Creating entirely new operators not already in the language
Giving additional meaning to existing operators when used with user-defined types

options: Implicitly the calling object (accessed via this)

The operator must remain a member function only

The operator has only one operand

questions.q: A virtual table (vtable) in C++ is:
options: A table storing all local variables of a function
A compiler-generated table of function pointers used to support dynamic dispatch of virtual functions
A user-defined data structure required for all classes
A table used only for static member functions

questions.q: Each object of a class with virtual functions typically contains:
options: A copy of all the function code
A hidden pointer (vptr) to the class's vtable
A duplicate of the base class

questions.q: Early binding (static binding) means that:
options: The function to be called is determined at runtime based on the object type
The function to be called is determined at compile time
Functions are bound only when the program exits
Binding never occurs for non-virtual functions

questions.q: Late binding (dynamic binding) means that:
options: The function call is resolved at compile time
The function call is resolved at runtime, typically via the vtable, based on the actual object type
Binding is performed by the preprocessor
It only applies to non-member functions

options: Ensure the correct derived class destructor is called when deleting an object through a base class pointer
Prevent the class from being inherited

questions.q: Does C++ have a dedicated 'interface' keyword like some other languages (e.g., Java)?
options: Yes, C++ has a built-in interface keyword
No, C++ does not have an interface keyword; the interface concept is simulated using abstract classes
No, C++ does not support interfaces in any form

questions.q: In C++, an interface-like class is typically implemented as:
options: A class with only private data members
An abstract class containing only pure virtual functions (and no data members or implemented functions)
A struct with static members only

questions.q: Compared to a general abstract class, a pure 'interface' style abstract class in C++:
options: May contain fully implemented member functions and data members
Typically contains only pure virtual functions, providing a contract with no implementation
Cannot be inherited by any class
Must contain at least one static member

questions.q: A class implementing an interface-like abstract class in C++ must:
options: Leave all pure virtual functions unimplemented
Provide concrete implementations for all inherited pure virtual functions to become instantiable
Redeclare the abstract class as a friend

questions.q: The main purpose of an abstract class acting as an interface is to:
options: Store large amounts of data efficiently
Define a common contract/behavior that multiple unrelated derived classes must implement
Avoid the use of constructors entirely

questions.q: Can an abstract class used as an interface have a constructor in C++?
options: No, abstract classes can never have constructors
Yes, an abstract class can have a constructor, which is called when a derived concrete object is created
Only if it has no pure virtual functions
Only if it is declared static

Object composition (or aggregation) typically represents which kind of relationship?
options: A 'has-a' relationship, where one class contains an object of another class as a member

questions.q: An example of composition would be:
options: A Car class inheriting from a Vehicle class
A Car class containing an Engine object as one of its data members
A Car class overloading the + operator
A Car class with only static members

questions.q: An example of inheritance would be:
options: A Car class that contains a Wheel object as a member
A SportsCar class deriving from a Car class, extending its behavior
A Car class using a friend function
A Car class with a private constructor

questions.q: Compared to inheritance, composition is often preferred in design when:
options: A strict 'is-a' relationship exists between two classes

questions.q: Aggregation is often described as a specialized form of association where:
options: The contained object's lifetime is entirely dependent on the container in every case
One object contains or is associated with another, but the contained object can often exist independently
No relationship exists between the two objects
The two classes must be in the same inheritance hierarchy

questions.q: Members declared as private in a class are accessible:
options: Only within the class itself (and its friends)

questions.q: Members declared as public in a class are accessible:
options: From anywhere the object is visible, including outside the class

questions.q: Members declared as protected in a class are accessible:
options: From anywhere in the program, just like public members
Within the class itself and its derived classes, but not generally from outside code
